title: Common Mistakes in System Design Interviews
summary: The recurring, avoidable ways candidates lose points in system design interviews, and the self-checks that catch them in the moment.

slides.markdown:
Most system design interview failures aren't caused by not knowing enough technology — they're caused by a small set of recurring, avoidable habits: designing before requirements are clear, over-engineering, hiding trade-offs, and ignoring the interviewer's cues.

Each one is individually easy to fix once you can recognize it happening, which is the point of this topic: not new technical knowledge, but a checklist of failure patterns and the self-checks that catch them mid-interview.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing before requirements are pinned down
slides.markdown:
Covered in depth in [clarifying requirements](clarifying-requirements), but it belongs on this list because it's still the single most common mistake: sketching an architecture before functional and non-functional requirements are settled, because the problem looks familiar.

The tell is a design that would be identical regardless of which answers the interviewer gave to your (few or zero) questions — if your architecture doesn't depend on anything you learned, you probably designed it before you actually needed the requirements.

Self-check: before drawing the first box, ask whether you could state the one or two numbers or constraints that most shape this specific design.

slides.sectionTitle: Over-engineering for scale the requirements never asked for
slides.markdown:
The opposite failure of skipping requirements is ignoring them once you have them — reaching for sharding, multi-region replication, and a message queue for a system the requirements described as a few thousand users. Interviewers notice complexity that doesn't trace back to a stated need just as readily as they notice missing complexity.

Over-engineering often comes from pattern-matching to "what a real, famous version of this system looks like" rather than to the specific numbers given in this interview. Twitter-at-scale and "design a Twitter clone for a 10,000-user community" call for very different architectures, even though they share a name.

Self-check: for every piece of distributed-systems complexity you add, be able to point at the specific number or requirement that necessitates it.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an over-engineered design vs a right-sized one for the same requirements
slides.markdown:
![Over-engineered design with sharding, layered caches, and a queue vs. a right-sized single-DB design for the same small-scale requirement](assets/overengineered-vs-rightsized.svg)

Both diagrams could be defended in isolation, but only one fits the stated requirement — and an interviewer who gave you a small-scale number is specifically checking whether the complexity of your design tracks the complexity of the problem.

The right-sized design isn't the "lesser" answer; matching complexity to actual need is itself the skill being evaluated here.

slides.sectionTitle: Never mentioning trade-offs — presenting one option as the only option
slides.markdown:
Related to the failure covered in [deep dives and trade-off discussions](deep-dives-and-trade-off-discussions), but broader: this mistake shows up across the whole interview, not just the deep dive, whenever a decision is stated as if no alternative existed. "I'll use a SQL database" with no reason given reads as a default, not a decision.

The fix doesn't require exhaustive comparisons at every step — one clause is often enough: "I'll use a SQL database here since we need transactional guarantees across these tables." That single phrase converts a bare assertion into a traceable choice.

Self-check: scan your own design for any component you introduced with no "because" attached, and add one.

slides.sectionTitle: Ignoring the interviewer's hints and steering questions
slides.markdown:
Interviewer questions during your design are rarely idle curiosity — "what happens if that node goes down?" is usually a pointed hint that failure handling is the thing worth addressing next, not a tangent to note and return to your prepared plan.

Candidates focused on executing their own mental script sometimes acknowledge a hint ("good point, I'll come back to that") and then don't, which reads as not listening rather than as time management. Treat almost every interviewer question as the single highest-priority thing to address next, ahead of whatever you'd planned to say.

If you genuinely need to finish a thought first, say so and then actually return to it: "let me finish this point, then I'll address failure handling" — and follow through within the next minute, not at the end of the interview.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: common failure patterns and the fix for each
slides.markdown:
The failures above cluster into a short, memorable set with a matching fix each.

| Failure | What it looks like | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Skipping requirements | Designing before asking questions | Two minutes of targeted questions first |
| Over-engineering | Distributed-systems complexity with no justifying number | Trace every addition to a stated requirement |
| Hiding trade-offs | "I'll use X" with no reason | Attach one "because" clause per decision |
| Ignoring hints | Noting a question, then not returning to it | Treat interviewer questions as top priority |

**How to decide:** run this table as a private mid-interview self-check at the halfway point — most candidates are doing at least one of these without noticing.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: memorized architecture recited without adapting to the given constraints
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I've studied the standard design for this exact system, so I'll reproduce it as given."

**Why it's wrong:** the standard write-up for "design Twitter" or "design an URL shortener" was built against a generic, unstated set of assumptions — this interview's actual requirements will differ in at least one dimension, and reciting the template ignores whatever that difference is. Interviewers often change one number specifically to see if the template gets adapted or repeated verbatim.

**Correct model:** use memorized designs as a starting library of components and trade-offs, not as a fixed answer — check each piece against this interview's specific numbers and constraints before including it, and be ready to explain why it changes if the constraints do.

slides.sectionTitle: The recovery move: course-correcting after you catch your own mistake
slides.subTitle: Self-correction
slides.markdown:
Making one of these mistakes isn't fatal — most interviewers expect you to stumble somewhere in 45 minutes. What actually costs points is not noticing, or noticing but not saying anything.

If you realize five minutes in that you skipped scoping non-functional requirements, say so out loud: "Let me back up — I jumped to the design before pinning down our latency budget, let me fix that." That single sentence often scores *better* than never having made the mistake, because it demonstrates the self-monitoring a staff engineer needs in a real design review, where nobody catches every gap on the first pass either.

**Testing:** whether you can catch and correct your own error mid-interview, not just avoid errors in the first place — self-correction under pressure is closer to the day-to-day skill than flawless execution.
